posts.post_title: The Compton metabolic profile test panel inc…
posts.post_content: The Compton metabolic profile test panel includes which of the following blood components to assess protein metabolism?

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Urea, Albumin, Hb

The correct answer is Urea, Albumin, Hb.

Correct Option Explanation

Urea, Albumin and Hb are the blood components chosen to reflect protein metabolism in the metabolic profile test.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • Blood glucose reflects energy metabolism, not protein status.
  • Ca, P and Mg reflect major mineral metabolism.
  • Na and K reflect electrolyte metabolism.
Know More
  • PCV and BUN are part of the Compton profile.
  • Cu, Co, Iodine assess trace element status.
  • The mini metabolic profile assesses only energy and protein intake.
  • A:G ratio is part of the total serum protein assessment.
  • Metabolic profile tests are ideally repeated bi-annually.

posts.post_title: In the interpretation of the metabolic profi…
posts.post_content: In the interpretation of the metabolic profile test, low blood glucose in a dairy cow is most closely associated with which condition?

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Ketosis

The correct answer is Ketosis.

Correct Option Explanation

Low blood glucose produces ketosis and is also responsible for poor conception rate in dairy cattle.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • Osteomalacia is a bone-softening disease of adults linked to Ca, P or vitamin D deficiency, not glucose.
  • Hypomagnesaemia is linked to low serum Mg, not glucose.
  • Parakeratosis is a skin condition linked to zinc deficiency.
Know More
  • Glucose is lower in early lactation and in winter months.
  • Stress and corticosteroids raise blood glucose.
  • Albumin and Hb decline reflects long-standing low protein status.
  • Globulin and total protein increase with age.
  • Mini profile testing is typically done 4–10 weeks after calving.

posts.post_title: Which mineral's serum level, when abnormally…
posts.post_content: Which mineral's serum level, when abnormally low in late pregnancy, is considered a dangerous indicator in the metabolic profile test?

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Calcium

The correct answer is Calcium.

Correct Option Explanation

Serum calcium varies within narrow limits, and abnormally low levels in late pregnancy indicate a dangerous situation predisposing to milk fever.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • Sodium is assessed along with K, Cu and selenium in pregnant animals, but is not the mineral flagged as dangerous in late pregnancy.
  • Potassium, like sodium, is part of the electrolyte panel but not specifically flagged for late pregnancy risk.
  • Iodine is assessed with Na, K, Cu and selenium, not singled out for late-pregnancy danger.
Know More
  • Phosphorus tends to fall after long-term insufficient intake.
  • Magnesium deprivation with cold weather causes clinical hypomagnesaemia.
  • Mg supplementation is protective against hypomagnesaemia.
  • Season and stage of lactation cause significant physiological fluctuations.
  • MPT is expensive and needs a regional laboratory with trained staff.

posts.post_title: Which of the following is a stated limitatio…
posts.post_content: Which of the following is a stated limitation of the metabolic profile test as a diagnostic tool?

_aimcq_options.text: It cannot be used in dairy herds
It requires a regional laboratory with automated equipment and trained staff
It is only applicable to horses

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: It requires a regional laboratory with automated equipment and trained staff

The correct answer is It requires a regional laboratory with automated equipment and trained staff.

Correct Option Explanation

A stated limitation of the metabolic profile test is the need for a regional laboratory with automated analytical equipment and trained staff, along with a local population database.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • The test is specifically designed for use in dairy herds, not excluded from them.
  • The test is described for ruminants broadly, not restricted to horses.
  • The test does assess mineral status including Ca, P and Mg.
Know More
  • MPT is a laboratory aid to preventive medicine.
  • It helps monitor fertility in relation to metabolic status.
  • It is useful at the end of winter and end of summer.
  • A satisfactory automated analytical method is preferred for choosing a metabolite.
  • Local, breed and location specific database is needed for interpretation.

posts.post_title: Milk fever in dairy cattle is caused by whic…
posts.post_content: Milk fever in dairy cattle is caused by which of the following conditions?

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Hypocalcemia

The correct answer is Hypocalcemia.

Correct Option Explanation

Milk fever is a disease of adult female bovines occurring around parturition, caused by hypocalcemia, and characterised by weakness, recumbency, paresis, shock and death.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • Hyperkalemia is not the defining cause; potassium changes are linked to creeper cow presentation instead.
  • Hyperphosphatemia is not the primary defect; serum phosphorus decreases, prolonging recumbency.
  • Hyponatremia is not described as the causal electrolyte disturbance in milk fever.
Know More
  • Milk fever mostly affects the 3rd to 7th calving group.
  • Jersey breed is most susceptible.
  • Majority of cases occur within 72 hours postpartum.
  • An alkaline diet increases incidence; an acid diet decreases it.
  • The Ca:Mg ratio in blood is normally about 6:1.

posts.post_title: Which breed of cattle is stated to be most s…
posts.post_content: Which breed of cattle is stated to be most susceptible to milk fever compared to other breeds?

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Jersey

The correct answer is Jersey.

Correct Option Explanation

Jersey cattle are the breed most susceptible to milk fever compared to other dairy breeds.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • Holstein is not identified as the most susceptible breed in the source.
  • Sahiwal is an Indian zebu breed not specifically flagged as most susceptible.
  • Gir is an Indian zebu breed not specifically flagged as most susceptible.
Know More
  • High susceptibility occurs with a high protein diet before and after calving.
  • There is no specific seasonal occurrence of milk fever.
  • Complete milking within the first 48 hours is a precipitating factor.
  • Certain families within a breed show more susceptibility.
  • Hypomagnesaemia decreases Ca mobilization from bone, precipitating milk fever.

posts.post_title: During which stage of milk fever does an aff…
posts.post_content: During which stage of milk fever does an affected cow show sternal recumbency with a lateral kink and subnormal temperature of 97–101°F?

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Stage II

The correct answer is Stage II.

Correct Option Explanation

Stage II of milk fever is characterised by sternal recumbency with lateral kink, a dry muzzle, cold extremities and subnormal temperature (97–101°F).

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • Stage I is the prodromal stage with excitement, tetany and hypersensitiveness, not recumbency.
  • Stage III shows lateral recumbency, coma and impalpable pulse, a more advanced presentation.
  • A convalescent stage is not one of the three defined clinical stages of milk fever.
Know More
  • Stage I shows grinding of teeth and a protruding tongue.
  • Stage III shows coma and flaccid limbs.
  • In Stage II the pupil is dilated with no reflex.
  • Untreated Stage III animals may die within 12–24 hours.
  • Death in the excitable form occurs due to respiratory failure.

posts.post_title: What is the recommended dose of calcium in a…
posts.post_content: What is the recommended dose of calcium in a cow undergoing treatment for milk fever?

_aimcq_options.text: 1 gm Ca per 45 kg (100 lb) body weight
5 gm Ca per 45 kg body weight
0.1 gm Ca per 45 kg body weight
10 gm Ca per 45 kg body weight

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: 1 gm Ca per 45 kg (100 lb) body weight

The correct answer is 1 gm Ca per 45 kg (100 lb) body weight.

Correct Option Explanation

The standard calcium dose for treating milk fever is 1 gm Ca per 45 kg (100 lb) of body weight, typically as calcium borogluconate.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • 5 gm/45 kg overstates the recommended dose.
  • 0.1 gm/45 kg understates the recommended dose.
  • 10 gm/45 kg overstates the recommended dose.
Know More
  • 25% calcium borogluconate contains 10.4 gm Ca per 500 ml.
  • Cattle are given 400–500 ml i/v and 100–200 gm s/c.
  • Goats receive 15–20 gm i/v.
  • Do not milk the cow for 6 hours after treatment.
  • If the cow does not stand after 24 hours, hip lifters are used.

posts.post_title: Which of the following is an unfavourable re…
posts.post_content: Which of the following is an unfavourable response observed during calcium therapy for milk fever?

_aimcq_options.text: Pulse rate decreasing with improved amplitude

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Cardiac irregularities

The correct answer is Cardiac irregularities.

Correct Option Explanation

Cardiac irregularities, increased heart rate and shallow respiration are unfavourable responses to calcium therapy, warranting caution during administration.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • Belching is a normal favourable response to calcium therapy.
  • Sweating of the muzzle is listed among the normal favourable responses.
  • A decreasing pulse rate with improved amplitude is a favourable sign of recovery.
Know More
  • A favourable response includes firm stool with mucous on defecation.
  • Urination typically does not occur until the cow rises.
  • Treatment is ideally started during Stage I of milk fever.
  • Feeding less than 20 g Ca/day for 2 weeks pre-partum helps prevent milk fever.
  • Vitamin D2 can be given at 20–30 million units/day antepartum for prevention.

posts.post_title: Which factor is described as decreasing the…
posts.post_content: Which factor is described as decreasing the incidence of milk fever through dietary management?

_aimcq_options.text: Feeding a high-calcium diet before calving
Feeding a high-protein diet before calving

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Feeding an acid diet

The correct answer is Feeding an acid diet.

Correct Option Explanation

An acid diet decreases the incidence of milk fever, whereas an alkaline diet increases it — the basis of the dietary cation-anion difference approach.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • An alkaline diet is stated to increase, not decrease, milk fever incidence.
  • Feeding high calcium before calving is discouraged; low Ca (<20 g/day) is recommended instead.
  • High-protein diet before and after calving increases susceptibility to milk fever.
Know More
  • Avoid drastic diet changes; allow 3–4 days for transition.
  • The dietary cation-anion difference (DCAD) programme is used preventively.
  • Complete milking in the first 48 hours can precipitate milk fever.
  • CaCl2 oral gel dosing (40–50 g) is used around calving.
  • 1,25(OH)2D3 can be given 10,000 IU i/m 24 hours prior to parturition.

posts.post_title: Which laboratory or postmortem finding suppo…
posts.post_content: Which laboratory or postmortem finding supports a diagnosis of ischemic muscle necrosis complicating milk fever?

_aimcq_options.text: Increased SGOT with pale muscle surrounded by normal-coloured muscle

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Increased SGOT with pale muscle surrounded by normal-coloured muscle

The correct answer is Increased SGOT with pale muscle surrounded by normal-coloured muscle.

Correct Option Explanation

Ischemic muscle necrosis (degenerative myopathy) is diagnosed post mortem by pale muscle surrounded by normal-coloured muscle, with an increased SGOT.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • Low serum phosphorus alone is a general finding in milk fever, not specific to ischemic necrosis.
  • Elevated blood glucose is not a described diagnostic finding for ischemic muscle necrosis.
  • Reduced serum magnesium alone reflects concurrent hypomagnesaemia, not muscle necrosis specifically.
Know More
  • Longer intervals between recumbency and treatment increase downer cow incidence.
  • Temperature above 39°C during treatment indicates a complicating condition.
  • Concurrent ketosis may cause a cow to rise after Ca therapy but remain ketotic.
  • History of access to oxalate-rich plants is part of the differential diagnosis.
  • Animals should be kept in sternal recumbency during treatment to avoid aspiration pneumonia.

posts.post_title: What is the typical duration after calving w…
posts.post_content: What is the typical duration after calving within which the majority of milk fever cases occur?

_aimcq_options.text: Within the last month of pregnancy only

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Within 72 hours postpartum

The correct answer is Within 72 hours postpartum.

Correct Option Explanation

The majority of milk fever cases occur within 72 hours after parturition, though some cases occur in the last days of pregnancy.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • 30 days postpartum is far beyond the typical window described for most cases.
  • Cases are not restricted purely to the last month of pregnancy; most occur after calving.
  • 6 months postpartum is well outside the described high-risk window.
Know More
  • High prevalence occurs during the 3rd–7th calving.
  • The 5–10 year age group is most commonly affected.
  • Ca:Mg ratio is normally about 6:1 in the body.
  • Coliform mastitis toxin can decrease serum Ca and P.
  • Increased estrogen interferes with Ca mobilization from bone.

posts.post_title: Which route of calcium administration is rec…
posts.post_content: Which route of calcium administration is recommended to be given slowly to avoid cardiac complications during milk fever treatment?

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Intravenous route

The correct answer is Intravenous route.

Correct Option Explanation

Calcium borogluconate is given 50% intravenously and 50% subcutaneously; the i/v portion must be given slowly to avoid precipitating cardiac irregularities.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • Oral calcium is not the standard emergency treatment route for acute milk fever.
  • Subcutaneous administration alone is used for part of the dose, but the i/v route is the one requiring slow, careful administration.
  • Intramuscular calcium is not the described treatment route; it can cause tissue necrosis.
Know More
  • The response to calcium includes muscle tremor spreading from flanks to the whole body.
  • Heart sound intensity increases with successful therapy.
  • Wait 5–8 hours before repeating the dose if the cow hasn't stood.
  • Placement on non-slippery ground or a rubber mat aids recovery.
  • The cow should not be milked for 6 hours post-treatment.

posts.post_title: In the reproductive tract, which of the foll…
posts.post_content: In the reproductive tract, which of the following complications is associated with milk fever?

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Uterine prolapse

The correct answer is Uterine prolapse.

Correct Option Explanation

Milk fever is associated with reproductive tract complications including dilated cervix, uterine prolapse, dystocia and retained placenta.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • Ovarian cysts are not among the reproductive complications listed for milk fever.
  • Vaginal atresia is a congenital defect, not a described milk fever complication.
  • Persistent corpus luteum is not listed as a milk fever complication.
Know More
  • Decreased muscle tone in milk fever increases vulnerability to prolapse.
  • Dystocia is also associated with milk fever.
  • Retained placenta can occur as a reproductive complication.
  • Hypothermia and depression of consciousness occur in the pathogenesis.
  • Phosphorus decrease can prolong the duration of recumbency.

posts.post_title: What is the primary purpose of feeding a low…
posts.post_content: What is the primary purpose of feeding a low-calcium diet (less than 20 g Ca/day) for two weeks prior to parturition?

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: To prevent milk fever

The correct answer is To prevent milk fever.

Correct Option Explanation

Feeding low Ca (<20 g/day) with normal phosphorus for 2 weeks before parturition is a preventive dietary measure against milk fever.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • Osteodystrophia fibrosa relates to chronic Ca:P:vitamin D imbalance, not this short-term prepartum measure.
  • Ketosis prevention relies on energy/propionate management, not low prepartum calcium.
  • Hypomagnesaemia prevention relies on magnesium supplementation, not calcium restriction.
Know More
  • The dietary cation-anion difference (DCAD) programme is another preventive strategy.
  • Sudden dietary changes should be avoided; allow 3–4 days transition.
  • Vitamin D2 antepartum dosing is 20–30 million units/day.
  • 1,25(OH)2D3 can be repeated at 24-hour intervals if delivery is delayed.
  • Oral CaCl2 gel (40–50 g) can be given around calving as prevention.

posts.post_title: Which sign is characteristic of Stage I (pro…
posts.post_content: Which sign is characteristic of Stage I (prodromal stage) of milk fever?

_aimcq_options.text: Grinding of teeth and muscular tremor of head and limbs

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Grinding of teeth and muscular tremor of head and limbs

The correct answer is Grinding of teeth and muscular tremor of head and limbs.

Correct Option Explanation

Stage I of milk fever is marked by excitement, hypersensitiveness, grinding of teeth and muscular tremor of the head and limbs.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • Coma and impalpable pulse describe Stage III, the most advanced form.
  • Sternal recumbency with lateral kink describes Stage II.
  • Bloat leading to death within 24 hours describes untreated Stage III.
Know More
  • Stage I animals are ataxic and fall easily.
  • Stage I animals are disinclined to eat and move.
  • Stage II shows a dry muzzle and cold extremities.
  • Stage III shows inaudible heart sounds around 120/min.
  • Treatment during Stage I is considered ideal.

posts.post_title: Concurrent ketosis in a milk fever case is s…
posts.post_content: Concurrent ketosis in a milk fever case is suggested by which clinical observation?

_aimcq_options.text: The cow rises after calcium therapy but continues to show signs of ketosis

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: The cow rises after calcium therapy but continues to show signs of ketosis

The correct answer is The cow rises after calcium therapy but continues to show signs of ketosis.

Correct Option Explanation

Concurrent ketosis is suspected when the animal rises after calcium therapy but continues to show signs of ketosis, indicating a second, separate metabolic problem.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • A temperature above 41°C is not specifically described as indicating concurrent ketosis; >39°C indicates a general complication.
  • Uterine prolapse is a reproductive tract complication, not an indicator of concurrent ketosis.
  • Joint swelling is not a described sign linking to concurrent ketosis in milk fever.
Know More
  • Milk fever with hypomagnesaemia and hyperphosphatemia shows tetany beyond Stage I.
  • History of access to oxalate-rich plants is part of the diagnostic work-up.
  • Ketosis diagnosis relies on hypoglycemia, ketonemia and ketonuria.
  • Serum Ca, Mg and P estimation supports the diagnosis of milk fever.
  • Death in the excitable milk fever form occurs due to respiratory failure.

posts.post_title: Which of the following best describes the pa…
posts.post_content: Which of the following best describes the pathogenesis of milk fever related to phosphorus levels?

_aimcq_options.text: A decrease in phosphorus prolongs the duration of recumbency
An increase in phosphorus shortens recovery time
Phosphorus levels have no effect on recumbency duration

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: A decrease in phosphorus prolongs the duration of recumbency

The correct answer is A decrease in phosphorus prolongs the duration of recumbency.

Correct Option Explanation

In the pathogenesis of milk fever, a decrease in serum phosphorus prolongs the duration of recumbency in affected cows.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • The source states a decrease, not increase, in phosphorus affects recumbency; an increase shortening recovery is unsupported.
  • Phosphorus is explicitly linked to prolonged recumbency, so it is not without effect.
  • Phosphorus excess causing uterine prolapse is not a described relationship.
Know More
  • Hyperaesthesia replaces hypersensitivity in the pathogenesis description.
  • If serum Mg decreases, tetany-like signs continue into Stage II.
  • Hypothermia and depression of consciousness occur in pathogenesis.
  • Decreased muscle tone increases prolapse vulnerability.
  • Normal Ca:Mg ratio in the body is about 6:1.

posts.post_title: Acute parturient hypocalcaemia in goats is b…
posts.post_content: Acute parturient hypocalcaemia in goats is basically due to a depression of which parameter in tissue fluid?

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Ionised calcium

The correct answer is Ionised calcium.

Correct Option Explanation

A depression of ionised calcium in tissue fluid is the basic biochemical defect underlying acute parturient hypocalcaemia in goats.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • Total protein is not identified as the basic biochemical defect.
  • Blood glucose is relevant to concurrent hypoglycemia in other species (e.g. bitches), not the goat's basic defect.
  • Serum sodium is not implicated as the basic defect in goats.
Know More
  • Milking goats are mostly affected during 4–6 years of age.
  • Cases can occur up to 3 weeks after parturition.
  • Treatment uses 25% calcium borogluconate 80–100 ml slow I/V.
  • Serum calcium in affected goats ranges from 2 to 6 mg/dl.
  • Pathogenesis is similar to dairy cows.

posts.post_title: Acute parturient hypocalcaemia (eclampsia) i…
posts.post_content: Acute parturient hypocalcaemia (eclampsia) in bitches most commonly occurs within which period after whelping?

_aimcq_options.text: Immediately at birth of the puppies

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: 2–10 days

The correct answer is 2–10 days.

Correct Option Explanation

Eclampsia in bitches is a metabolic disease occurring commonly in young bitches within 2–10 days of whelping.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • 4–8 weeks post-whelping is outside the typical onset window described.
  • 6 months is far beyond the described acute onset period.
  • Onset is described as occurring after whelping, not immediately at birth of puppies.
Know More
  • Predisposing factors include toy breeds and heavy litter size.
  • Concurrent hypoglycemia contributes to tonic-clonic convulsions.
  • Serum calcium below 7 mg/dl is diagnostic.
  • Blood glucose below 80 mg/dl is also diagnostic.
  • Treatment includes removing the suckling puppies.

posts.post_title: In canine eclampsia, what is the recommended…
posts.post_content: In canine eclampsia, what is the recommended treatment dose of 25% calcium borogluconate?

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: 1 ml/kg body weight slow I/V

The correct answer is 1 ml/kg body weight slow I/V.

Correct Option Explanation

In canine eclampsia, 25% calcium borogluconate is given at 1 ml/kg body weight, administered slow intravenously.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • 10 ml/kg overstates the recommended dose by an order of magnitude.
  • Oral administration is not the described route for acute treatment.
  • Intramuscular administration is not the described route; the drug is given slow I/V.
Know More
  • 20% dextrose 30–50 ml slow I/V is also given for concurrent hypoglycemia.
  • Diazepam 0.5 mg/kg b.wt slow I/V is used to control fits.
  • Predisposing factors include improper prenatal nutrition.
  • Low blood glucose (<80 mg/dl) reflects concurrent hypoglycemia.
  • Clinical signs include opisthotonus and hyperthermia.

posts.post_title: Lactation tetany in mares (transit tetany) m…
posts.post_content: Lactation tetany in mares (transit tetany) most commonly occurs around which time relative to foaling?

_aimcq_options.text: About the 10th day of foaling or 1–2 days after weaning
Immediately at the time of foaling

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: About the 10th day of foaling or 1–2 days after weaning

The correct answer is About the 10th day of foaling or 1–2 days after weaning.

Correct Option Explanation

Lactation tetany in mares occurs in lactating mares at about the 10th day of foaling or 1–2 days after weaning.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • Onset is not described as immediate at the time of foaling itself.
  • 6 months after foaling is well beyond the described onset window.
  • The condition occurs postpartum during lactation, not before foaling.
Know More
  • Mortality rate in lactation tetany can be as high as >60%.
  • Mares grazing on lush pasture with heavy milk flow are more susceptible.
  • Serum Ca <5 mg% is associated with recumbency and stupor.
  • Main sign of recovery is voiding large volumes of urine.
  • Differential diagnosis includes tetanus and laminitis.

posts.post_title: In lactation tetany of mares, a serum calciu…
posts.post_content: In lactation tetany of mares, a serum calcium level below 5 mg% is associated with which clinical presentation?

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Recumbency and stupor

The correct answer is Recumbency and stupor.

Correct Option Explanation

In lactation tetany of mares, serum Ca >8 mg% shows excitability, 5–8 mg% shows spasm, and <5 mg% is associated with recumbency and stupor.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • Excitability corresponds to serum Ca above 8 mg%, not below 5 mg%.
  • Spasm corresponds to serum Ca between 5 and 8 mg%, not below 5 mg%.
  • Clinical signs are explicitly present at this level, contrary to this option.
Know More
  • Handling can precipitate tetany in affected mares.
  • There is a distinct thumping sound from the chest due to diaphragm spasm.
  • Death may occur 48 hours after onset of illness.
  • Peristalsis is reduced in lactation tetany.
  • Complete recovery follows injection of calcium solutions.

posts.post_title: Which of the following differentiates tetanu…
posts.post_content: Which of the following differentiates tetanus from lactation tetany in mares?

_aimcq_options.text: Tetanus shows prolapse of the membrane nictitans with no relation to foaling or weaning
Tetanus always occurs 10 days after foaling
Tetanus responds rapidly to calcium therapy
Tetanus is characterised by voiding large volumes of urine

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Tetanus shows prolapse of the membrane nictitans with no relation to foaling or weaning

The correct answer is Tetanus shows prolapse of the membrane nictitans with no relation to foaling or weaning.

Correct Option Explanation

Tetanus is differentiated by prolapse of the membrane nictitans and no relationship to recent foaling, weaning or physical exertion.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • Occurring 10 days after foaling is characteristic of lactation tetany, not tetanus.
  • Rapid response to calcium therapy is characteristic of lactation tetany, not tetanus.
  • Voiding large urine volumes is the recovery sign of lactation tetany, not a feature of tetanus.
Know More
  • Laminitis differential shows anxiety, muscle tremor and foot pain.
  • Lactation tetany shows no prolapse of membrane nictitans.
  • Draft horse breeding is commonly associated with lactation tetany.
  • Precipitating factors include hard physical work and prolonged transport.
  • Recovery sign is voiding large volumes of urine.

posts.post_title: Which factor predisposes young bitches to ec…
posts.post_content: Which factor predisposes young bitches to eclampsia according to the described predisposing factors?

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Heavy litter size

The correct answer is Heavy litter size.

Correct Option Explanation

Heavy litter size is listed as a predisposing factor for eclampsia in bitches, along with toy breeds and improper prenatal nutrition.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • Large breed size is not listed; toy breeds are specifically mentioned as predisposed.
  • Old age at first whelping is not a listed predisposing factor; young bitches are affected.
  • Excess dietary phosphorus alone is not listed; inappropriate calcium supplementation is the relevant factor.
Know More
  • Toy breeds are specifically predisposed to eclampsia.
  • Atony of smooth and skeletal muscle is a predisposing factor.
  • Concurrent hypoglycemia causes tonic-clonic convulsions.
  • Clinical signs include poor maternal care and salivation.
  • Treatment removes suckling puppies to reduce calcium drain.

posts.post_title: What is the treatment of choice for acute pa…
posts.post_content: What is the treatment of choice for acute parturient hypocalcaemia in goats?

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: 25% Calcium Borogluconate 80–100 ml slow I/V

The correct answer is 25% Calcium Borogluconate 80–100 ml slow I/V.

Correct Option Explanation

Acute parturient hypocalcaemia in goats is treated with 25% Calcium Borogluconate at 80–100 ml, given slow intravenously.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • Oral bone meal is a preventive phosphorus supplement, not the treatment for acute hypocalcaemia.
  • Vitamin D2 alone is used as a preventive measure in cattle, not the direct treatment described for goats.
  • Insulin is used in diabetes mellitus treatment, unrelated to hypocalcaemia.

  • Response to therapy is rapid in goats.
  • Serum calcium in goats ranges 2–6 mg/dl when affected.
  • Milking goats 4–6 years of age are most affected.
  • Cases may occur even 3 weeks after kidding.

posts.post_title: In canine eclampsia, which of the following…
posts.post_content: In canine eclampsia, which of the following clinical signs reflects concurrent hypoglycemia rather than hypocalcaemia alone?

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Tonic-clonic convulsions

The correct answer is Tonic-clonic convulsions.

Correct Option Explanation

Concurrent hypoglycemia is specifically stated as the cause of the signs of tonic-clonic convulsions in eclamptic bitches.

  • Panting is a general clinical sign of eclampsia, not specifically attributed to hypoglycemia.
  • Restlessness is a general clinical sign of eclampsia, not specifically attributed to hypoglycemia.
  • Poor maternal care is a general clinical sign of eclampsia, not specifically attributed to hypoglycemia.

  • Eclampsia synonyms include puerperal tetany.
  • Stiff tilted gait is due to muscular tetany.
  • Clinical signs include opisthotonus.
  • Low blood glucose in eclampsia is defined as less than 80 mg/dl.
  • 20% dextrose is given 30–50 ml slow I/V for hypoglycemia.

posts.post_title: Which statement about lactation tetany in ma…
posts.post_content: Which statement about lactation tetany in mares is correct regarding mortality?

_aimcq_options.text: Mortality is negligible in all cases
Mortality rate can be greater than 60%
Mortality is unrelated to treatment delay

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Mortality rate can be greater than 60%
